title: The Last Language
premise: Oscar Oyelaran, a bridge inspector drifting through a loveless marriage, hears a song on the radio that he knows was written by his late mother and never recorded—proof someone has been singing her stolen work for decades. Following the melody back to Lagos, where his family's publishing empire collapsed amid betrayal, he uncovers the truth: his father sold her songs to a rising star and erased her from the family story. As his mother's dementia advances and the singer's estate prepares a hagiographic biography, Oscar must choose between protecting his inheritance of silence and giving his mother back her voice. In the end he publishes her notebooks under her own name, loses his marriage but finds his own, and sings one verse at her bedside as she briefly remembers everything.
about_author: K. M. Oyelaran is the pen name of a Nigerian-British writer who spent six years working as a structural engineer before turning to fiction. Their stories examine the quiet violence families commit in the name of legacy.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Oscar inspects a failing bridge while mentally measuring the gaps in his own marriage to Denise; POV Oscar. A radio plays an unfamiliar song whose lyrics he knows by heart—his mother's unpublished lullaby. The emotional beat is vertigo: the discovery that his carefully invisible life rests on a hidden fracture.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Oscar says nothing to Denise, instead digging through his late mother Adaeze's boxes: notebooks of songs, letters cut short mid-sentence. His father's old business partner calls, warning him not to 'stir old water.' POV Oscar. The beat is dread mixed with longing—the first pull toward a past he fled.

chapters.title: What Papa Sold
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter from young Oscar's perspective, 1989 Lagos: he witnesses his father hand Adaeze's songbook to a hungry young musician named Femi Sau, calling it 'a loan between friends.' Young Oscar stays silent when his mother asks if anyone has seen it. The beat is inherited guilt taking root.

chapters.title: Return Ticket
chapters.summary: Oscar lies to Denise about a work conference and flies to Lagos, where Adaeze lives with his sister Ngozi and is losing words daily. He hears her hum fragments she can no longer name. POV Oscar. The beat is tenderness sharpened by urgency—time is literally erasing the evidence.

chapters.title: Femi Sau's House
chapters.summary: Oscar confronts the aging superstar, now a national treasure preparing a museum of his career. Femi is charming, evasive, then quietly menacing: 'Your father gave. I took nothing.' POV Oscar. The beat is power revealing its teeth—corruption dressed as gratitude.

chapters.title: Ngozi's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ngozi reveals she has spent years documenting their mother's authorship but lacked standing—and courage—to act. She shows Oscar royalty statements routed through shell companies their father controlled until his death. POV Ngozi. The beat is sisterhood forged in shared anger, and the cost of waiting.

chapters.title: Denise Calls
chapters.summary: Denise, having found the lie, arrives unannounced—not to fight but because she recognizes the song too; her own mother sang it to her. Their marriage cracks open into honesty for the first time in years. POV Denise. The beat is grief becoming intimacy: two people discovering they were both tenants.

chapters.title: The Museum Opening
chapters.summary: At the televised gala launching Femi's legacy museum, Oscar publicly asks about the provenance of the hit song 'Adanwa.' Femi's denial collapses when a recording of Adaeze singing the original, made by Oscar's father, plays over the sound system—Ngozi's doing. POV Oscar. The beat is the climax: truth detonating in a room built on myth.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Lawsuits, headlines, and Femi's fall; Oscar faces what exposure has cost him and whether it was worth it. Adaeze, shown the newspaper, reads her own name aloud twice. POV Ngozi. The beat is reckoning—victory that feels like loss until Adaeze's small recognition reframes everything.

chapters.title: Adanwa
chapters.summary: Months later, Adaeze's collected songs are published under her name; Oscar and Denise have separated gently, honestly. At her bedside, Oscar sings 'Adanwa' and Adaeze joins him, word-perfect, for one full verse before slipping back. POV Oscar. The beat is resolution: inheritance reclaimed not as property but as voice, passed on.
